overview.summary: Industrial designers design products that are made in large numbers, such as phones, chairs, appliances, tools and vehicles, so that they work well, look good and can be produced affordably.
overview.problems: They make everyday products easier, safer and more enjoyable to use.
overview.worksWith: Engineers, marketing teams, manufacturers, users and other designers.
overview.workplaces: Design studios, manufacturing companies, consultancies and in-house design teams.

timeline.title: Research and observation
timeline.description: The designer watches how people use similar products and notes their frustrations.
timeline.why: Good design starts with real use.

timeline.title: Sketching ideas
timeline.description: The designer draws many quick concepts.
timeline.why: Many rough ideas lead to better final ones.

timeline.title: Developing concepts
timeline.description: The designer builds 3D models in software and makes simple physical mock-ups.
timeline.why: Holding a model shows what a drawing cannot.

timeline.title: Testing with people
timeline.description: The designer lets users try mock-ups and notes the problems.

timeline.title: Working with engineers and makers
timeline.description: The designer checks materials, costs and how a design can be manufactured.
timeline.why: A design has to be possible to make.

timeline.title: Deadlines and revisions
timeline.why: Few designs survive unchanged from first sketch to factory.

challenges: Ideas must fit budgets, safety rules and manufacturing limits.
Competition is strong and portfolios matter.
Compromises with engineering and marketing are constant.
Waste and environmental impact are increasingly part of the job.
workEnvironment: Studios and workshops, with computers, sketching and model-making, plus meetings and visits to factories or users. Hours are usually regular, with extra effort before deadlines.
rewards: Seeing products you designed in use
A mix of art and engineering
tradeoffs: Pay and opportunities that vary by country and industry

activity.title: Redesign an everyday object
steps: Choose a simple object, such as a water bottle or a school bag, and watch two people use it, noting any problems.
Pick one and make a quick model from cardboard, paper and tape.
Ask someone to try it and say what is awkward.
activity.outcome: You practise observing users, sketching ideas, making a model and improving it.
activity.safety: Use only paper, cardboard and tape, ask an adult for help with scissors, and avoid hot glue or sharp tools without supervision.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
